country.name: Morocco
country.tagline: The Arab world's leading quality producer, with an AOC in the Atlas foothills and a national love of vin gris.

stats.note: Wikipedia: about 50,000 ha of vines in the early 2000s, most for table grapes; wine production about 400,000 hl in 2013.

country.overview:
Morocco grew vines in Roman times (the ruins of Volubilis, near Meknès, have olive presses and Bacchic mosaics) and again under the French protectorate from 1912, when colonists planted around Meknès, Fès, Rabat and Casablanca. Production peaked above 3 million hectolitres in the 1950s. After independence (1956) the EEC's quotas of 1967 cut exports, and from 1973 the state took over most vineyards; quality fell until the 1990s, when the state company SODEA leased land to foreign investors, mainly French, such as Castel and William Pitters.

The central figure of modern Moroccan wine was Brahim Zniber (about 1920 to 2016), who built Celliers de Meknès and the Diana Holding group into a business that by 2016 controlled about 85 percent of national production and some 8,300 hectares. His Château Roslane, near Meknès, became in 2009 the first estate with 'château' status, and its vineyards make up the country's only AOC, Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru (2001).

Morocco has about 14 AOG zones (appellation d'origine garantie) grouped into five regions, from Berkane and Angad in the east to Guerrouane, Beni M'tir and Zerhoune around Meknès, Zemmour and Zaër near Rabat, and Doukkala inland from El Jadida. Most wine is red, from Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah, but the national style is vin gris, a very pale rosé from Cinsault and Grenache, the best-selling wine in a country where sale to Muslims is technically forbidden and consumption is concentrated in cities, hotels and among tourists. Castel's Boulaouane was for years the best-selling foreign wine in France.

history.title: Roman Volubilis
history.text: The Roman city near Meknès had presses and Bacchic mosaics; the region's wine and oil were traded across the empire.

history.title: The protectorate vineyard
history.text: French settlers planted around Meknès, Fès, Rabat and Casablanca; output passed 3 million hl in the 1950s.

history.title: State control and foreign revival
history.text: The state took over vineyards in 1973; from the 1990s SODEA leased them to French investors.

history.title: Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru
history.text: Morocco's first and only AOC was created for vineyards of Celliers de Meknès around Château Roslane.

country.classification: Morocco's system, set up from the 1970s and revised in the 1990s and 2000s, has about 14 AOG zones (appellations d'origine garanties) and one AOC, Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru. 'Château' status for single estates was first granted to Château Roslane in 2009.
country.climate_soils: Mediterranean with Atlantic influence on the coast; the Meknès plateau at 500 to 700 metres and the Middle Atlas foothills are cooler and get 500 to 600 mm of rain. Soils are clay-limestone and sandy; the eastern zones near Berkane are drier.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: The most planted wine grape, base of vin gris.

ma-angad.name: Angad
ma-angad.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-angad.summary: The Angad plain around Oujda in the far east. One of Morocco's driest wine areas, near the Algerian border, it makes sturdy reds from Carignan, Cinsault and Grenache. It is one of the three AOGs of the Oriental region with Berkane and Beni Sadden.

ma-beni-mtir.name: Beni M'tir
ma-beni-mtir.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-beni-mtir.summary: Plateau south of Meknès at around 700 to 800 metres, among the coolest and highest Moroccan vineyards, including the area around Boufekrane and El Hajeb. The altitude and cool nights give fresher reds and some of Morocco's best whites, and Château Roslane's AOC vineyards lie at its edge.

ma-beni-sadden.name: Beni Sadden
ma-beni-sadden.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-beni-sadden.summary: A small eastern zone. It is one of the three eastern AOGs, with Berkane and Angad, in Morocco's dry Oriental region. Its exact boundaries and producers could not be verified for this atlas.

ma-berkane.name: Berkane
ma-berkane.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-berkane.summary: Eastern zone near the Mediterranean and the Algerian border, around Berkane; reds and rosés. The Moulouya plain and the Beni Snassen foothills have a Mediterranean climate, warmer and drier than the Meknès plateau. Wineries here make mostly reds and rosés.

ma-chellah.name: Chellah
ma-chellah.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-chellah.summary: Named after the Roman and Merinid site of Chellah at Rabat; vineyards on the coastal hinterland. The Rabat and Casablanca hinterland was one of the main vineyard areas of the French protectorate, close to the big urban markets.

ma-coteaux-de-latlas-1er-cru.name: Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru
ma-coteaux-de-latlas-1er-cru.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-coteaux-de-latlas-1er-cru.summary: Morocco's only AOC, created in 2001 for vineyards of Celliers de Meknès on the Meknès plateau around Château Roslane, at about 600 to 700 metres in the foothills of the Middle Atlas; mainly red blends of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah aged in oak.

ma-doukkala.name: Doukkala
ma-doukkala.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-doukkala.summary: Inland from El Jadida around Boulaouane, whose Castel-owned brand was long France's best-selling imported wine. The sandy Doukkala plain is hot and flat, and most of its wine is red and rosé for the domestic and French markets.

ma-gharb.name: Gharb
ma-gharb.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-gharb.summary: The fertile Gharb plain around Sidi Slimane north-east of Kenitra. The fertile alluvial plain behind the Atlantic coast is better known for citrus, rice and sugar beet, and its wines are mostly everyday reds and rosés.

ma-guerrouane.name: Guerrouane
ma-guerrouane.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-guerrouane.summary: A large AOG west of Meknès known for vin gris and soft reds; Les Celliers de Meknès and Castel source much of their wine here. Clay-limestone soils at around 500 to 600 metres and Atlantic air from the west give softer wines than the hotter east.

ma-sahel.name: Sahel
ma-sahel.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-sahel.summary: Coastal zone south of Casablanca. It is one of the five AOGs of the Rabat and Casablanca region, with Atlantic-influenced vineyards. Its exact boundaries could not be verified for this atlas.

ma-saiss.name: Saïss
ma-saiss.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-saiss.summary: The Saïss plain between Meknès and Fès. The plateau lies at around 500 to 600 metres, and its clay-limestone soils supply the large Meknès wineries, mainly with reds and vin gris.

ma-zaer.name: Zaër
ma-zaer.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-zaer.summary: South-east of Rabat around Rommani and Benslimane, home of Thalvin's Domaine des Ouled Thaleb. Sandy soils and Atlantic breezes give the zone fresh rosés and vin gris as well as reds.

ma-zemmour.name: Zemmour
ma-zemmour.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-zemmour.summary: Inland from Rabat around Khémisset. The plateau around Khémisset, between Rabat and Meknès, at 300 to 500 metres, makes reds and vin gris for the large Moroccan wineries. It is one of the five Rabat and Casablanca AOGs.

ma-zenata.name: Zenata
ma-zenata.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-zenata.summary: Coastal hills between Casablanca and Mohammédia, with Atlantic influence. It makes mainly reds and rosés for the Casablanca market, and urban growth has eaten into its vineyards.

ma-zerhoune.name: Zerhoune
ma-zerhoune.grapes: Cinsault, Carignan, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
ma-zerhoune.summary: Hills around Moulay Idriss Zerhoun and the Roman ruins of Volubilis north of Meknès. Vines grew here in Roman times around Volubilis. Today the zone gives reds and rosés from Cinsault, Grenache, Syrah and Cabernet.

sites.name: Château Roslane
sites.text: The Celliers de Meknès flagship estate in the foothills of the Middle Atlas near El Hajeb, granted Morocco's first château status in 2009; its vineyards make AOC Coteaux de l'Atlas 1er Cru.

sites.name: Volubilis
sites.text: Roman city near Meknès (UNESCO) with olive presses and Bacchic mosaics, at the centre of today's Zerhoune and Guerrouane wine zones.

sites.name: Domaine des Ouled Thaleb (Thalvin)
sites.text: One of Morocco's oldest wineries, founded in the 1920s near Benslimane in the Zaër zone, run by Thalvin.

sites.name: Boulaouane
sites.text: Kasbah village in the Doukkala whose name became the brand of Morocco's most exported wine.

sites.name: Meknès
sites.text: Imperial city of the Alaouite sultan Moulay Ismail and the capital of Moroccan wine, seat of Celliers de Meknès, the company Brahim Zniber built into the producer of about 85 percent of the country's wine by 2016. Most AOG zones of the Saïss plateau surround it.
